items.readable_text:
Content:
In a previous lesson, we learned how to compute Laplace transforms. We now examine how the Laplace transform changes when a function is multiplied by an exponential.

Content:
Suppose
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=F(s)]
exists for [MATH: s>s_0.] We want to compute the Laplace transform of [MATH: e^{at}f(t).]

Content:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform,
[MATH: L{e^{at}f(t)}|= ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{− st}e^{at}f(t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{− (s − a)t}f(t)dt.]

Content:
Now recall that
[MATH: F(s)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{-st}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t,
\qquad s>s_0.]
Comparing the two integrals, we see that
[MATH: \int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t
=F(s-a).]

Content:
For this to make sense, we need [MATH: s-a>s_0,] which is equivalent to
[MATH: s>s_0+a.]

Content:
This result is known as the First Shifting Theorem:
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\{e^{at}f(t)\} = F(s-a).]
In the next slide, we will apply this result to a concrete example.

items.readable_text:
Content:
The First shifting Theorem states that if
[MATH: \mathcal L\{f(t)\}=F(s)]
for [MATH: s>s_0], then
[MATH: \mathcal L\{e^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a),
\qquad s>s_0+a.]

Content:
So, when you multiply a function by [MATH: e^{at}], you do two things:

Content:
- Replace [MATH: s] with [MATH: s-a] in the known transform [MATH: F(s)].
- Shift the domain from [MATH: s>s_0] to [MATH: s>s_0+a].

Content:
To see this in action, consider the following example.

Content:
We are given that
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\{\sin(\omega t)\}=\frac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2},
\qquad s>0.]
Suppose we want to compute
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\{e^{2t}\sin(3t)\}.]

Content:
First, we identify the base transform:
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\{\sin(3t)\}=\frac{3}{s^2+3^2}]

Content:
Next, we apply the first shifting theorem with [MATH: a=2], which means we replace [MATH: s] by [MATH: s-2]:
[MATH: L{e^{2t}\sin (3t)}|= (3)/((s − 2)^{2} + 3^{2}); = (3)/((s − 2)^{2} + 9).]

Content:
Since the original transform is valid for [MATH: s>0], the shifted transform is valid for
[MATH: s>2.]

Content:
This example illustrates the general pattern: multiplying by [MATH: e^{at}] leads to a simple substitution [MATH: s:= s-a], along with a corresponding shift in the domain.

items.title: Applying the First Shifting Theorem

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: \mathcal{L} \left\{t\sin(\omega t) \right\}=\dfrac{2\omega s}{(s^2+\omega^2)^2},] find the Laplace transform [MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{e^{-5t}\cdot t\sin(2t)\right\}.]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: \mathcal{L} \left\{t\sin(\omega t) \right\}=\dfrac{2\omega s}{(s^2+\omega^2)^2},] find the Laplace transform [MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{e^{-5t}\cdot t\sin(2t)\right\}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The first shifting theorem states that if [MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),] then [MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\} = F(s-a).]

Using the given result, we have [MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{t\sin(2t) \right\} = \frac{2(2)s}{(s^{2}+2^2)^{2}}.]

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

[MATH: L{e^{− 5t} ⋅ t\sin (2t)}|= (2(2)(s + 5))/(((s + 5)^{2} + 2^{2})^{2}); = (4(s + 5))/(((s + 5)^{2} + 4)^{2}).]

items.title: Applying the First Shifting Theorem and Linearity

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: L{t^{n}}|= (n!)/(s^{n + 1}),|s > 0,] use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of [MATH: g(t) = 2t^2 + 5te^{4t}] for [MATH: s > 4.]
sections.readable_text:
Given that
[MATH: L{t^{n}}|= (n!)/(s^{n + 1}),|s > 0,]
use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of [MATH: g(t) = 2t^2 + 5te^{4t}] for [MATH: s > 4.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

[MATH: L{g(t)}|= L{2t^{2} + 5te^{4t}}; = L{2t^{2}} + L{5te^{4t}}; = 2L{t^{2}} + 5L{te^{4t}}]

We are given that, for [MATH: s > 0,] [MATH: L{t^{n}}|= (n!)/(s^{n + 1}).]

Therefore, we have the following: [MATH: L{t}|= (1)/(s^{2}); L{t^{2}}|= (2)/(s^{3})]

The first shifting theorem states that if [MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),] then [MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\} = F(s-a).] Therefore, [MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{ te^{4t} \right\} = \dfrac{1}{(s-4)^2}.]

Therefore, the Laplace transform of [MATH: g(t)] is

[MATH: L{g(t)}|= 2L{t^{2}} + 5L{te^{4t}}; = 2 ⋅ (2)/(s^{3}) + 5 ⋅ (1)/((s − 4)^{2}); = (4)/(s^{3}) + (5)/((s − 4)^{2}).]

This transform is valid for [MATH: s>4.]

This transform is valid for [MATH: s>4.]

sections.normalized_html: Consider a function [MATH: f(t)] for which the Laplace transform is [MATH: \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s).] How can we obtain the graph of [MATH: \mathcal{L}\{e^{-6t} f(t)\}] from the graph of [MATH: F(s)?]
sections.readable_text: Consider a function [MATH: f(t)] for which the Laplace transform is [MATH: \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s).] How can we obtain the graph of [MATH: \mathcal{L}\{e^{-6t} f(t)\}] from the graph of [MATH: F(s)?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The first shifting theorem states that if [MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),] then [MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\} = F(s-a).]

This implies that multiplying a function [MATH: f(t)] by [MATH: e^{at}] shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the [MATH: s]-axis.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In a previous lesson, we learned how to compute Laplace transforms. We now examine how the Laplace transform changes when a function is multiplied by an exponential.

Content:
Suppose
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=F(s)]
exists for [MATH: s>s_0.] We want to compute the Laplace transform of [MATH: e^{at}f(t).]

Content:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform,
[MATH: L{e^{at}f(t)}|= ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{− st}e^{at}f(t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{− (s − a)t}f(t)dt.]

Content:
Now recall that
[MATH: F(s)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{-st}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t,
\qquad s>s_0.]
Comparing the two integrals, we see that
[MATH: \int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t
=F(s-a).]

Content:
For this to make sense, we need [MATH: s-a>s_0,] which is equivalent to
[MATH: s>s_0+a.]

Content:
This result is known as the First Shifting Theorem:
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\{e^{at}f(t)\} = F(s-a).]
In the next slide, we will apply this result to a concrete example.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Using the First Shifting Theorem

Content:
The First shifting Theorem states that if
[MATH: \mathcal L\{f(t)\}=F(s)]
for [MATH: s>s_0], then
[MATH: \mathcal L\{e^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a),
\qquad s>s_0+a.]

Content:
So, when you multiply a function by [MATH: e^{at}], you do two things:

Content:
- Replace [MATH: s] with [MATH: s-a] in the known transform [MATH: F(s)].
- Shift the domain from [MATH: s>s_0] to [MATH: s>s_0+a].

Content:
To see this in action, consider the following example.

Content:
We are given that
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\{\sin(\omega t)\}=\frac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2},
\qquad s>0.]
Suppose we want to compute
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\{e^{2t}\sin(3t)\}.]

Content:
First, we identify the base transform:
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\{\sin(3t)\}=\frac{3}{s^2+3^2}]

Content:
Next, we apply the first shifting theorem with [MATH: a=2], which means we replace [MATH: s] by [MATH: s-2]:
[MATH: L{e^{2t}\sin (3t)}|= (3)/((s − 2)^{2} + 3^{2}); = (3)/((s − 2)^{2} + 9).]

Content:
Since the original transform is valid for [MATH: s>0], the shifted transform is valid for
[MATH: s>2.]

Content:
This example illustrates the general pattern: multiplying by [MATH: e^{at}] leads to a simple substitution [MATH: s:= s-a], along with a corresponding shift in the domain.

---

Item 3 — Example: Applying the First Shifting Theorem

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: \mathcal{L} \left\{t\sin(\omega t) \right\}=\dfrac{2\omega s}{(s^2+\omega^2)^2},] find the Laplace transform [MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{e^{-5t}\cdot t\sin(2t)\right\}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The first shifting theorem states that if
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),]
then
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\} = F(s-a).]

Using the given result, we have
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{t\sin(2t) \right\} = \frac{2(2)s}{(s^{2}+2^2)^{2}}.]

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

[MATH: L{e^{− 5t} ⋅ t\sin (2t)}|= (2(2)(s + 5))/(((s + 5)^{2} + 2^{2})^{2}); = (4(s + 5))/(((s + 5)^{2} + 4)^{2}).]

---

Item 6 — Example: Applying the First Shifting Theorem and Linearity

Example Prompt:
Given that
[MATH: L{t^{n}}|= (n!)/(s^{n + 1}),|s > 0,]
use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of [MATH: g(t) = 2t^2 + 5te^{4t}] for [MATH: s > 4.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

[MATH: L{g(t)}|= L{2t^{2} + 5te^{4t}}; = L{2t^{2}} + L{5te^{4t}}; = 2L{t^{2}} + 5L{te^{4t}}]

We are given that, for [MATH: s > 0,]
[MATH: L{t^{n}}|= (n!)/(s^{n + 1}).]

Therefore, we have the following:
[MATH: L{t}|= (1)/(s^{2}); L{t^{2}}|= (2)/(s^{3})]

The first shifting theorem states that if [MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),] then [MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\} = F(s-a).] Therefore,
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{ te^{4t} \right\} = \dfrac{1}{(s-4)^2}.]

Therefore, the Laplace transform of [MATH: g(t)] is

[MATH: L{g(t)}|= 2L{t^{2}} + 5L{te^{4t}}; = 2 ⋅ (2)/(s^{3}) + 5 ⋅ (1)/((s − 4)^{2}); = (4)/(s^{3}) + (5)/((s − 4)^{2}).]

This transform is valid for [MATH: s>4.]

---

Item 9 — Tutorial: Graph Shifting

Content:
Recall that the first shifting theorem states that if
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),]
then
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\} = F(s-a).]

Content:
This means the new Laplace transform is the original graph of [MATH: F] evaluated at [MATH: s-a].

Content:
So, the graph shift is:

Content:
- If [MATH: a>0], then [MATH: F(s-a)] is the graph of [MATH: F(s)] shifted to the right by [MATH: a] units.
- If [MATH: a<0], then [MATH: F(s-a)] is the graph of [MATH: F(s)] shifted to the left by [MATH: |a|] units.

Content:
For example, suppose [MATH: F(s)] has the following graph:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/482a97d677ae52b2473f2ce4e5713abd]

Content:
Then the Laplace transform of [MATH: e^{-3t} f(t)] is [MATH: F(s+3).] Here, [MATH: a=-3], so this corresponds to shifting the graph of [MATH: F(s)] three units to the left:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d4d101c27cce5fb1b5698f442f5b5e6c]

Content:
A useful self-check is that any horizontal features move the same way:

Content:
- vertical asymptotes shift left/right by the same amount,
- intercepts and key points shift left/right by the same amount.

---

Item 10 — Example: Identifying Graph Shifts From the First Shifting Theorem

Example Prompt:
Consider a function [MATH: f(t)] for which the Laplace transform is [MATH: \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s).] How can we obtain the graph of [MATH: \mathcal{L}\{e^{-6t} f(t)\}] from the graph of [MATH: F(s)?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The first shifting theorem states that if
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),]
then
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\} = F(s-a).]

This implies that multiplying a function [MATH: f(t)] by [MATH: e^{at}] shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the [MATH: s]-axis.

- If [MATH: a > 0,] the graph of [MATH: F(s)] shifts to the right.
- If [MATH: a < 0,] the graph of [MATH: F(s)] shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of [MATH: \mathcal{L}\{e^{-6t} f(t)\},] we must shift the graph of [MATH: F(s)] by [MATH: 6] units to the left.

Item 13 — Example: Proving the First Shifting Theorem

Example Prompt:
Consider a function [MATH: f(t)] such that its Laplace transform is [MATH: \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)] for [MATH: s>s_0.] Suppose we wish to find [MATH: \mathcal{L}\{e^{-7t} f(t)\}.] Show the steps to compute this transform.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

[MATH: L{e^{− 7t}f(t)}|= ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{− st} ⋅ e^{− 7t}f(t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{∞}e^{− (s + 7)t}f(t)dt]

Now, recall that [MATH: \displaystyle F(s) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-st} \, f(t)\, \textrm{d}t,] where [MATH: s > s_0.] Therefore,
[MATH: \int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s+7)t} \, f(t)\, \textrm{d}t = F(s+7),]
where
[MATH: s + 7 > s_0
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
s > s_0 - 7.]

Item 16 — Tutorial: A Laplace Transforms Comparison Table

Content:
Using the first shifting theorem, we can obtain new Laplace transforms from old ones without performing any additional integration.

Content:
If
[MATH: \mathcal L\{f(t)\}=F(s)]
for [MATH: s>s_0], then
[MATH: \mathcal L\{e^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a),
\qquad s>s_0+a.]

Content:
The table below shows some general results we can obtain using the first shifting theorem.

Content:
| [MATH: f(t)] | [MATH: F(s)=\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\}] | Compare With |
| [MATH: e^{at} t^n] | [MATH: \dfrac{n!}{(s-a)^{n+1}}] | [MATH: \mathcal L \{t^n\} = \dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}] |
| [MATH: e^{at}\sin \omega t] | [MATH: \dfrac{\omega}{(s-a)^2+\omega^2}] | [MATH: \mathcal L\{\sin\omega t\} = \dfrac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2}] |
| [MATH: e^{at}\cos \omega t] | [MATH: \dfrac{s-a}{(s-a)^2+\omega^2}] | [MATH: \mathcal L\{\cos\omega t\} = \dfrac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}] |

Content:
So, each new entry in our table is obtained by taking a known transform and replacing [MATH: s] with [MATH: s-a], and then shifting the domain accordingly.
